title: Capacity Planning
description: Learn to forecast resource needs, right-size Linux servers, and avoid capacity-related outages through proactive planning.

data.text: Capacity planning answers a simple question: will our systems handle next quarter's traffic? Without planning, growth becomes a series of emergencies. With planning, growth becomes a series of deliberate investments.
This lesson covers CPU, memory, disk, and network forecasting on Linux, plus how to translate metrics into purchase and architecture decisions.
Capacity is not just CPU. A system can be CPU-rich but starved for disk I/O or memory bandwidth. Measure all four constraints and identify the bottleneck before scaling.

data.text: Capacity forecasting blends historical data with business projections. Start with current utilization trends, then apply expected growth rates and seasonal patterns.

items: Collect utilization data for at least 30 days
Calculate daily and weekly growth rates
Identify seasonal peaks such as Black Friday or end-of-month billing
Project resource exhaustion dates using linear regression or moving averages
Add a 20% buffer for unexpected traffic spikes

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: Vertical scaling (bigger machines) is simpler to plan but creates single points of failure. Horizontal scaling (more machines) is more resilient but requires load balancing and stateless design.
Load testing validates capacity plans before they become production problems. Use tools such as `wrk`, `hey`, or `k6` to simulate realistic traffic patterns and observe where systems break.

data.title: Simple HTTP load test with wrk

wrk -t12 -c400 -d30s --latency https://api.example.com/health

items: Baseline current resource utilization over 30 days
Define growth assumptions with the product team
Run load tests before every major launch
Document right-sizing decisions in architecture reviews

data.title: Summary
data.text: Capacity planning prevents surprise outages by aligning infrastructure investments with real demand. Track CPU, memory, disk, and network, forecast using historical data, validate with load tests, and always keep a buffer for the unexpected.
